Kierkegaard’s greatness lies in the fact that he recognized the great figures of the German awakening, Goethe and Hegel, as brothers made from gently living flesh—as traitors to the spirit, which indeed they were: the Hegel of the Phenomenology of Spirit—I would like to know whether Kierkegaard ever read it at all—and the Goethe of the Urfaust.
It is the hump that builds itself a spirit. And it is into the hump constructed in this way by the spirit that the psychoanalysts crawl like bedbugs.
The old, experienced brothel madam—wise in her own way, tactful and discreet; she has served kings—is looking for fresh flesh. She calls this: the lay apostolate. Now she is running after the Jews.
“And powers of delusion, hating without restraint, Begin to disappear, blindly hurling beasts.”

One of these beasts hurled blindly is poor Peter Schneider of Zurich, Switzerland—hurled out in order to refute me quickly, while the powers of delusion that hate one another without restraint are already beginning to disappear.
A fine entry for the hundredth anniversary of Søren Kierkegaard’s death.

A Christian cannot leave this earth as a demigod, or even as a hero. But suppose this ambitious Peter Schneider really did catch me. Then all that would be needed would be the decent resolve to make oneself impossible to classify once again for these dogcatchers and distributors of dog tags.
16 November 1955, Day of Repentance and Prayer
We are very slow to catch on.
It took us 150 years to read Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit.
It took us 100 years to understand Hölderlin.
When will we understand lines such as these by Theodor Däubler, from Hymn to Sicily?
And powers of delusion, hating without restraint, Begin to disappear, blindly hurling beasts.
One of these blindly hurled beasts is Simone Weil.
Would I be allowed to write that to Karl Epting?
If I recite a line like that to one of today’s big shots, he smiles and says:
“Very interesting phonetically. The first line is built around the vowel A, the second around I. It also makes sense in terms of the intellectual content.”
Better think about who the beasts blindly hurled by different powers of delusion might be:
Adolf Hitler, Roosevelt—better stop now, or you will be arrested at once.
I have gone through my whole life without property.
My lack of property corresponded to my lack of illusions.
Psychologically speaking, however, my lack of illusions came first.
Given my profession, I could have become a property owner without much difficulty.
Out of contempt for false security.
Out of revulsion at the concrete forms in which property presented itself to me.
So I am the propertyless jurist.
Let someone else try to match that.
Better stop now, or you will be arrested at once.
It is about the struggle between intoxicating drugs.

What do you use to intoxicate yourself? I chew clubmoss spores! Then you are a pig! And what do you use to intoxicate yourself? I drink wine! But the priests have taken that away from you! It still tastes good to me!
The fact that it still tastes good to you is irrelevant.
You live in a community where you are allowed to drink wine only under the table—outside the sacrament. So your pleasure in wine is a private matter.
The poor celibate bureaucracy drinks the wine openly. But it is no longer capable of any intoxicant; of any marriage; of any asceticism. It lives in its monasteries like people in caves <…>
Down, then, into the underworld with it and all its concubinages-concordats!!
Do they too fall into the underworld along with this celibate bureaucracy?

What makes Simone Weil representative is the superiority of this Jewish girl who managed to escape every effort of the professional makers of converts and left them all standing behind her with stupid looks on their faces.
And it is more beautiful than the art of Edith Stein, who allowed herself to be baptized and then became impenetrable inside a religious order.
I wrote this to Karl Epting.

Simone Weil’s horror at the idea of the Corpus Christi, the Body of Christ, is genuine. But it is also the one decisive test: anyone who does not want to belong to the Corpus Christi is not a Christian and does not want to be one, even though that person may still want to speak about Christian matters and impress Christians.
Epting thinks the doctrine of the Corpus mysticum, the mystical body, is not Lutheran.
I look it up in Sohm’s Church Law, §34, and find that it is of the highest importance in Luther.
Christ is the head, not the Pope.
According to Sohm, the opposition is:
Corpus Christi versus Corpus Antichrist = Leviathan (= state = Sohm, p. 674).
This economic miracle is only a miracle of repentance; when repentance ends, the miracle ends.
This state is only a state of repentance, or, as [Franz] Böhm says, a reparations state; when repentance ends, the state ends with it.
And then surely morality as well: when repentance ends, morality ends with it.

And then none of it is true anymore—including the Christianity of the C-parties and all the established and officially recognized values, together with those who assign those values and those who cash them in: the preachers of repentance who persecute others instead of supplying the only proof of truth of which, according to Kierkegaard, a preacher of repentance is capable: allowing himself to be beaten to death.
“For to be the great preacher of repentance means to be beaten to death.” (The Concept of the Chosen One, p. 303.)
But they live in the economic miracle which, as I said, is a miracle of repentance—and vice versa.
Of course the song is not finished yet.
Certainly: when repentance ends, the miracle ends.
That is how they threaten us Germans.
But we threaten them back: when the miracle ends, repentance ends, and with it the whole beautiful Caux co-existence!
Then the preachers of repentance will no longer be able to travel around in their Mercedes Apostolorum and will turn back into honest black-market petrol dealers.
Bombers above my cap, both my feet deep inside the camp. Around me, the ugliness of the victors, and the sound-wave hell of their radio hits.
I am losing the time that loses itself and gaining the time that exists. For I experience and shape concrete concepts.
And powers of delusion, helplessly hating one another, Begin—blindly hurling beasts—to disappear.
Hitler was one such blindly hurled beast, but he was not the only one and not the last. And before he disappeared, he in turn blindly hurled beasts of his own and bound his enemies to his shadow.

To speak about this without falling oneself into the unrestrained hatred of those powers of delusion; without oneself being turned into one of those blindly hurled beasts; without theological-demonological cozy talk and without some hidden motive concerning reparations—that is difficult and dangerous. For the moment, the blindly hurled, the blind haters and avengers, still control the field and allow no objective word to be spoken.

One need only look at the disgusting falsifications that dominate Baron von der Heydte’s article in Hochland, January/February 1951. Above all there is the central and revealing falsification in his quotation of my sentence about prayer as the final refuge, from Ex Captivitate Salus, p. 61. He silently leaves out the crucified God. He simply suppresses Him.
By doing so, he strips the sentence of its concrete Christian meaning.
It is as though someone removed a crucifix from a room in order to deceive the visitors.

Informers like to smuggle false documents or pieces of evidence into rooms that are about to be searched. Here someone does the reverse: he makes a piece of evidence disappear. And that piece of evidence is the crucified God.

There is no pleasant taste on your tongue, no pleasure of eye or ear, that does not carry a long history inside it—indeed, the history of your entire physical existence from the moment of conception, and probably from much earlier still.
Analysis is no use here. Only the concept can help.
The essence of the human being is historical.
Every second of the present, though it seems to disappear immediately, has been prepared far in advance and continues to have effects far into the future.
Every moment of the most fleeting pleasure is a compendium of everything we have ever been and everything we will ever be.
Pain is the Other, the alien thing.
It is too unrelated for that.
But the Christian ought to be on the side of pain.
Take a look at Christians from that point of view.
